title: Saladin and the Ayyubid Sultanate
welcome_lead: Meet Salah ad-Din Yusuf ibn Ayyub — Saladin — who united Egypt and Syria and reshaped the medieval Near East.

walkthroughs.body_html: Born in 1137 or 1138 in Tikrit, Saladin entered the service of Zengid ruler Nur ad-Din. Despatched to Egypt, he gradually displaced the declining Fatimid Caliphate, abolishing it in 1171 and recognising the Abbasid caliph. After Nur ad-Din's death in 1174 Saladin extended his authority across Syria and northern Mesopotamia, presenting himself as champion of Sunni unity.

On 4 July 1187 Saladin lured the Crusader army under King Guy of Lusignan into a waterless plateau at the Horns of Hattin and destroyed it, capturing the True Cross. Within months he had retaken Jerusalem (October 1187), allowing Christian inhabitants to ransom themselves — a striking contrast to the Latin sack of 1099.

Although Richard I forced Saladin to relinquish part of the coast, Jerusalem remained Muslim until 1229. Saladin died in Damascus in 1193, reportedly leaving little personal wealth. His chivalrous reputation appears in Christian as well as Muslim sources, and the Ayyubid dynasty endured until displaced by the Mamluks in 1250.

mcqs.q: Why did William the Conqueror commission the Domesday Book in 1086?
options: It was a list of Anglo-Saxon rebels William wanted to execute.
It was a census of the English population, like a modern one.
Gandhi insisted on partition to ensure Hindu dominance.
To record landholding and resources so he could assess taxation (geld), confirm Norman tenants' rights, and settle disputes over confiscated Anglo-Saxon estates.
Gandhi insisted on partition to ensure Hindu dominance.
Hindus and Muslims had always hated each other so partition was inevitable.
It was a list of Anglo-Saxon rebels William wanted to execute.
The Muslim League's demand for Pakistan, Congress refusal of power-sharing, communal violence, British haste to leave, and Mountbatten's accelerated timetable.

mcqs.q: Why did Huguenots migrate to England from the 1680s?
options: It was a list of Anglo-Saxon rebels William wanted to execute.
Huguenots were Catholic refugees fleeing Cromwell.
Huguenots came to England because France was poorer than England.
Louis XIV's 1685 revocation of the Edict of Nantes ended toleration of French Protestants; many fled persecution to Protestant England, bringing skills like silk weaving.
